clues.text: This tissue was first transplanted successfully between identical twins in the 1950s, work that won E. Donnall Thomas a share of the 1990 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Four years after receiving this tissue from a German donor, a Reno sheriff's office employee learned in 2019 that his semen carried only the donor's DNA.
About 400,000 years ago, people in Israel's Qesem Cave kept skin-wrapped deer legs for up to nine weeks before cracking them open to eat this.
This soft, spongy tissue in the hollow centers of the skeleton makes roughly 500 billion blood cells a day, and transplants of it are used to treat leukemia.

bone-marrow.writerNotes: Clue 1: the NAS biographical memoir (Appelbaum, 2021) says matching was 'at first limited to identical twins' and that Thomas and Ferrebee reported their first identical-twin marrow transplants in 1959; Britannica dates the first successful twin transplant to 1956. Hence the hedge 'in the 1950s'. Nobel 1990 shared with Joseph Murray (kidney) per Wikipedia. Clue 2: Chris Long, IT employee at the Washoe County Sheriff's Office (ABA Journal, citing NYT Dec 2019). He had a vasectomy, so the 'semen' contained only donor white blood cells; the clue says only that it 'carried only the donor's DNA', which all sources state. Clue 3: Blasco et al., Science Advances, 9 Oct 2019; metapodials of fallow deer kept with skin on; behavior dated c. 420,000-200,000 years ago, headline figure 400,000. Clue 4: ~500 billion/day per Wikipedia (Nombela-Arrieta & Manz 2017) and BioNumbers (~5x10^11 cells/day).

clues.text: Researchers in Madagascar reported in 2007 that a moth slips its barbed, harpoon-like proboscis under the closed eyelids of sleeping birds to drink this fluid.
In a 2011 Weizmann Institute study, men who sniffed this odorless fluid, donated by women, had lower testosterone and rated women's faces as less sexually appealing.
Bogorad's syndrome makes people whose facial nerve regrows wrongly after Bell's palsy produce this fluid while eating, and it is nicknamed after a reptile.
Made by the lacrimal glands, this salty fluid drains through tiny holes at the inner corners of the eyelids into the nose, which is why crying gives you a runny nose.

tears.writerNotes: Clue 1: moth is Hemiceratoides hieroglyphica; Hilgartner et al., Biology Letters, published January 2007 (Wikipedia says the behaviour was discovered in 2006, hence 'reported in 2007'). Wikipedia calls the proboscis 'harpoon-like'; Mongabay says 'sharply barbed'. The paper's authors think it slides between the lids rather than piercing them, so the clue says 'under the closed eyelids'. Clue 2: Gelstein et al., 'Human tears contain a chemosignal', Science 331 (Jan 2011), Noam Sobel's lab at the Weizmann Institute. The tears were collected from women watching sad films; I left the sad films out so the clue is not instant. Science News reports lower salivary testosterone and lower ratings of the sexual appeal of women's faces. Clue 3: I gave no year for Bogorad's paper because sources disagree (Wikipedia says 1926, a review says 1928). Radiopaedia describes the mechanism as misdirected regenerating fibres reaching the tear gland instead of the salivary gland. The 'reptile' is the crocodile (the condition is known as crocodile tears syndrome). The word 'tears' cannot appear in any clue, so that name is only hinted at. Clue 4: drainage through the puncta into the nose is in Wikipedia and Popular Science. The 'Tear' alias means no clue may use the bare word 'tear'.

clues.text: About 2% of people are born with Meckel's diverticulum, a pouch on this organ left over from the embryo's yolk stalk, which medical students remember by a 'rule of twos'.
A 2014 Swedish study found the gut's inner lining covers about 30 to 40 m², nearer half a badminton court than the oft-quoted tennis court, and most of that lies in this organ.
The middle section of this organ, the jejunum, is named from the Latin for 'fasting' because anatomists usually found it empty after death; the word 'jejune' shares the root.
This coiled tube between the stomach and the colon, lined with millions of finger-like villi, is where most of the nutrients from our food are absorbed.

small-intestine.writerNotes: Clue 1: prevalence is the textbook ~2% (Wikipedia notes true range 0.2-4%), hence 'about'. Clue 2: Helander & Fändriks, Scand J Gastroenterol 2014;49(6):681-9 (PMID 24694282). Total ~32 m² per BioNumbers (small intestine 30 m², large 1.9 m²); press coverage gives 30-40 m² and quotes the paper's 'half a badminton court' vs 'tennis lawn'. Wikipedia's own Small intestine page cites it as 2015 (online vs print); the journal issue is 2014. Clue 3: Wikipedia Jejunum: from Latin jējūnus 'fasting', 'so called because this part of the small intestine was frequently found to be void of food following death'; notes 'jejune' shares the root. Deliberately avoided giving a length, since sources disagree (Wikipedia Small intestine says ~3-5 m living; Jejunum page says 6-7 m).

clues.text: In 2022 London police took over 'Rewritten', a fan-run copy of this closed kids' game, after a Disney copyright complaint, and arrested three people.
In this online game's final weeks in 2017, players raced to get banned fastest by swearing in chat, with the best times from signup to ban under 40 seconds.
Disney bought this virtual world, made in Kelowna, British Columbia, for $350 million in 2007, plus up to $350 million in bonuses it never paid because profit goals were missed.
In this snowy online world for kids, launched in 2005, players waddled around as cartoon birds, decorated their igloos and kept fluffy pets called puffles.

club-penguin.writerNotes: Clue 1: the City of London Police's Intellectual Property Crime Unit (PIPCU) took over the Club Penguin Rewritten site on 13 April 2022; police said three people were arrested on 12 April 'on suspicion of distributing materials infringing copyright' (NME; Wikipedia). 'London police' = City of London Police. Clue 2: Wikipedia: 'The fastest times were under 40 seconds, with a tool-assisted speedrun (TAS) of 29 seconds.' Gigazine (Feb 2017) reported a 37.37 s record at the time. Clue 3: Wikipedia: bought August 2007 for $350M (precisely $350.93M) with up to $350M more if targets were met by 2009; 'Disney ultimately didn't pay the extra $350 million, as Club Penguin missed both profit goals.' New Horizon Interactive was a spin-off of Kelowna-based RocketSnail Games. Clue 4: launched 24 Oct 2005; Wikipedia: 'Each player was provided with an igloo for a home'; puffles were in-game pets.

clues.text: This web service was code-named Caribou, after a project in a 'Dilbert' strip, and at launch ran on 300 old Pentium III computers nobody else at its company wanted.
Paul Buchheit, who also suggested the corporate motto 'Don't be evil', built the first rough version of this service in a day, as a search tool for his own messages.
Launched on April 1, 2004, this service was widely taken for a hoax, and invitations to its early test version soon sold on eBay for $150 or more.
Google's free email service launched with 1 GB of storage, 500 times Hotmail's, and in Germany and the UK it had to call itself 'Google Mail' for years.

gmail.writerNotes: All of clues 1-3 rest mainly on Harry McCracken's 2014 Time feature: 'originally code-named Caribou', a name borrowed from Dilbert; 'running on three hundred old Pentium III computers nobody else at Google wanted'; Buchheit's first useful version (a search engine for his own email) 'did indeed take only a day'; many took the April 1 press release for a hoax; 'Bidding for invites on eBay sent prices shooting up to $150 and beyond'; 1 GB was '500 times what Microsoft's Hotmail offered'. Wikipedia (Paul Buchheit) confirms he suggested 'Don't be evil' in a 2000 meeting (Amit Patel coined it in 1999, so the clue says 'suggested', not 'coined'). Clue 4: UK rebrand to Googlemail until the dispute was resolved in May 2010 (Computerworld); German trademark transferred to Google in April 2012 (PCWorld). The display form was 'Googlemail'/'Google Mail'; the clue's 'Google Mail' does not contain the banned string 'gmail'.

clues.text: This company's famous yodel was recorded by country singer Wylie Gustafson for about $590; after it aired nationally, he sued for $5 million and settled in 2002.
This company turned down a chance to buy Google for $1 million in 1998, and in 2008 rejected Microsoft's $44.6 billion takeover bid.
Its founders said they picked its name for the slang sense 'rude, unsophisticated, uncouth', after the brutish humanlike creatures in 'Gulliver's Travels'.
Stanford grad students Jerry Yang and David Filo started this web portal in 1994 as 'Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web'.

yahoo.writerNotes: Clue 1: The Hustle says he accepted a one-time payment of $590.38 for what was meant to be a regional spot, then heard it nationally during the January 1999 Super Bowl; he asked for $5 million. The Register (23 Apr 2002) confirms the $5 million suit and the undisclosed settlement. Recording year is 1996 per several reports (The Hustle implies c. 1996-97), so the clue gives no year for the recording. Clue 2: Wikipedia: Page and Brin offered to sell for $1 million in 1998 and Yahoo declined; Microsoft's unsolicited $44.6 billion bid in Feb 2008 was rejected (Microsoft withdrew in May 2008). Clue 3: Wikipedia quotes the founders on 'rude, unsophisticated, uncouth' and the Gulliver's Travels origin. Clue 4: Wikipedia: Jan 1994, 'Jerry and David's guide to the World Wide Web', renamed in March 1994. Alias 'Yahoo' normalizes to the same string as the answer; kept as the assignment suggested.

clues.text: This 2012 track's opening 'Con los terroristas!' was sampled without permission from reggaeton star Héctor Delgado, who had quit music in 2008 for evangelical Christianity.
This track debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the very week the chart began counting YouTube views, only the 21st song ever to start at the top.
In 2013 up to 15 Australian miners were fired, and the FAA looked into a Frontier Airlines flight, after people filmed themselves doing this craze.
In this 2013 video craze set to a Baauer track, one person in a helmet or mask dances alone until the bass drops, then the video cuts to a whole room going wild in costumes.

harlem-shake.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia (Héctor el Father): announced his retirement from music on 3 Sept 2008 after becoming a born-again Christian, and confirmed his 'Los terroristas' clip was used uncredited in the opening of the song; Spin (Feb 2013) says he left music in 2008 to devote himself to evangelical Christianity. Wikipedia (song) says neither vocal sample was cleared; Diplo settled in April 2013. The song article traces the vocal to a remix of his 2006 single 'Maldades', Spin to 'Los Terroristas', so the clue names no source song. Clue 2: Complex: 'just the 21st song to debut at #1 on the Hot 100', the week YouTube data was added; Wikipedia agrees. Clue 3: Canadian HR Reporter (Reuters copy): Barminco fired 'up to 15 workers' at the Agnew mine, Western Australia, and the FAA was looking into a mid-air aisle performance on a Frontier flight. Clue 4: format per Wikipedia (meme), which credits the helmet/jump-cut form to TheSunnyCoastSkate's copy of Filthy Frank's video. No clue uses 'harlem' or 'shake'.

clues.text: This picture book topped the 'favorite childhood books' George W. Bush's office listed in a 1999 survey of governors, drawing jokes since it came out when he was in his twenties.
U.S. printers balked at this 1969 picture book's die-cut holes and pages of varying widths, so its editor found a printer in Japan to make it.
This book's author defended its use of 'cocoon' instead of 'chrysalis' by recalling his father telling him to come out of his cocoon: 'poetry won over science!'
In Eric Carle's picture book, a tiny larva eats through one apple, two pears, three plums and a huge Saturday feast, gets a stomach ache, then becomes a beautiful butterfly.

very-hungry-caterpillar.writerNotes: Clue 1: the Washington Examiner says Bush's office answered a 1999 Pizza Hut survey of governors on 'favorite childhood books' with a stock list that put this book first, and commentators mocked it because he was an adult when it came out. The Examiner says 23. By the dates (Bush born 6 July 1946, book published 3 June 1969) he was 22, so the clue says 'in his twenties'. Clue 2: Lithub says U.S. printers said they couldn't do the job, citing holes and pages of varying sizes. Penguin says no U.S. printer could handle the die-cut holes and irregular bindings, and that Ann Beneduce took it to Kaisei-sha in Japan. Wikipedia says U.S. printing of the holes was expensive. Clue 3: 'poetry won over science!' is Carle's own wording on his official FAQ, which also mentions his father's 'come out of your cocoon'. The words 'very', 'hungry' and 'caterpillar' appear in no clue.

clues.text: In 1926 the barrister C. P. Sanger showed that this novel's events can be dated exactly, between 1771 and 1803, and that its plot to take over two estates is legally sound.
For an 1850 edition of this novel, published after its author's death, her sister corrected the punctuation and diluted the thick Yorkshire dialect of the old servant Joseph.
Kate Bush, who shares a birthday with this novel's author, wrote a song named after it at 18 and became the first woman to top the UK chart with an entirely self-written song.
In this Emily Brontë novel, filmed in 2026 with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi, the foundling Heathcliff loves Catherine Earnshaw on the Yorkshire moors.

wuthering-heights.writerNotes: Clue 1: Sanger's essay 'The Structure of Wuthering Heights' (Hogarth Essays, 1926). Sanger quoted on the legal page: 'The period of the tale is from 1771 to 1803'; 'Emily Brontë clearly had a considerable knowledge of the law'; he traces how Heathcliff legally gets both the Heights (as mortgagee in possession) and Thrushcross Grange (via an entail and his son). Modernist Archives lists Sanger (1871-1930) as barrister and economist. 'Legally sound' is my paraphrase of Sanger's verdict; a checker may prefer 'and that its plot follows inheritance law closely'. Wikipedia: Sanger's chronology 'affirmed Emily's literary craft and meticulous planning'. Clue 2: Wikipedia: 'In 1850 Charlotte Brontë edited the original text for the second edition... She addressed the faulty punctuation and orthography but also diluted Joseph's thick Yorkshire dialect.' Emily died Dec 1848. Clue 3: Wikipedia (song): written aged 18 on 5 March 1977; she 'shared her birthday with its author' (30 July); 'Bush became the first female artist to have an entirely self-written number one in the UK.' Clue 4: Emerald Fennell's film, released 13 Feb 2026 (Robbie as Cathy, Elordi as Heathcliff).

clues.text: This 1952 children's book's illustrator, Garth Williams, first gave its heroine a woman's face, until the author asked him to draw her realistically.
When its author recorded this book for an audiobook in 1970, he reportedly needed 17 takes to read its heroine's death without his voice breaking.
Its author carried a spider's egg sac from his Maine barn to New York in a candy box, where the hatchlings escaped and strung silk from his hairbrush to his mirror.
In this E. B. White novel, a barn spider saves the pig Wilbur from slaughter by spinning words such as 'Some Pig' and 'Terrific'.

charlottes-web.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia: 'Williams's first drawings showed a spider with a woman's face. White suggested he draw a realistic spider instead'; Mental Floss adds he even tried a Mona Lisa look. Clue 2: the 17 takes come from biographer Michael Sims via NPR (2012, syndicated on WAMC) and are repeated by CSM and Wikipedia; hedged with 'reportedly'. Clue 3: NPR (2011, syndicated on WFAE): White put the egg sac in an empty candy box with air holes and left it on his bedroom bureau in New York; the spiderlings escaped and spun 'from his hair brush to his nail scissors to his mirror'. NPR dates the barn episode to fall 1949, Wikipedia to October 1950, so the clue gives no year. The clue avoids the word 'web' throughout.

clues.text: In 1953 the head of Vienna's kindergartens published a pamphlet calling this folklore figure 'an evil man' and warning that he could scar children for life.
In Styria this figure was said to hand families a bundle of birch twigs painted gold, which they hung up all year as a reminder to children to behave.
Austrian holiday cards since the 1800s often show this figure with a long tongue, one human foot and one cloven hoof, sometimes chasing after women.
On the night of December 5, this horned, hairy Alpine demon roams with St. Nicholas, swatting naughty children with birch switches and hauling the worst away in a basket.

krampus.writerNotes: Clue 1: Mental Floss says that in 1953 the head of Vienna's kindergarten system published a pamphlet calling him 'an evil man' and warning he could scar children for life. Wikipedia instead says the Austrian government handed out pamphlets titled 'Krampus Is an Evil Man' in the 1950s, so the sources differ on who issued it. A Goethe-Institut transcript (seen only in search results) also mentions a 1953 school administrator trying to ban him from kindergartens. If a checker wants it safer, change '1953 the head of Vienna's kindergartens' to 'the 1950s Austrian officials'. Clue 2: Wikipedia, and Mental Floss citing a 1958 article; both describe the twigs as gold-painted and kept all year as a reminder. Clue 3: Mental Floss covers the long tongue, the one human foot and one cloven hoof, and the chasing of women. The LOC Folklife blog dates the cards to 1885 to WWI and mentions cards of him wooing women. I chose these over the Dollfuss-era ban because sources disagree on the ban's dates (1932 vs 1934). The words Krampusnacht, Krampuslauf and Krampuskarten all contain the answer, so I avoided them.

clues.text: Naples was first called Parthenope, after one of these mythical creatures whose body was said to have washed ashore there after she threw herself into the sea.
When the Argonauts sailed past these creatures, Orpheus drowned out their voices with his own music, though one crewman, Butes, still leapt overboard.
In 1819 Charles Cagniard de la Tour named his new noise-making device after these creatures, because it could produce sound underwater.
Odysseus had his crew plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the mast so he could hear these singers safely; a crowned, twin-tailed one is Starbucks' logo.

sirens.writerNotes: Alias 'Siren' bans the substring 'siren' everywhere, so no clue names the device or the logo directly. Clue 1: Wikipedia History of Naples: the siren 'washed ashore at Megaride', having 'thrown herself into the sea after she failed to bewitch Ulysses with her song'; OUP blog: the Cumaean settlement was first named Parthenope after the siren, later Palaepolis next to Neapolis. 'Was said to' hedges the legend. Clue 2: Wikipedia: Orpheus drowned out their voices with his own playing; Butes 'leapt into the sea' (rescued by Aphrodite). Clue 3: Wikipedia (alarm): 'In 1819, an improved siren was developed and named by Baron Charles Cagniard de la Tour'; it 'could produce sound under water', hence the name. John Robison built an earlier version before 1799, so the clue says he named it, not that he invented the first one. Clue 4: Starbucks (2011, quoted by Stark Insider): the logo came from 'a 16th century Norse woodcut of a twin-tailed mermaid, or Siren'.

clues.text: One of this legendary pair is said to have vanished in a sudden thunderstorm while reviewing his army, and was later worshipped as the god Quirinus.
To settle which of them would name and rule a new city, this pair watched the sky from two hills; one saw six vultures first, but the other then saw twelve.
Figures of this pair were added to a famous bronze in Rome's Capitoline Museums in the late 15th century, and radiocarbon tests suggest the animal above them is medieval.
Set adrift on the Tiber as babies, these twin sons of Mars were suckled by a she-wolf; one later killed the other and founded Rome.

romulus-and-remus.writerNotes: Clue 1: Livy 1.16 (Roberts translation on Perseus): a violent thunderstorm enveloped the king in a cloud during a review of the army on the Campus Martius and 'From that hour Romulus was no longer seen on earth.' Quirinus identification goes back to Ennius (Wikipedia, Quirinus); hence 'later worshipped as'. Clue 2: Livy 1.6-7 via Wikipedia (Romulus: 'Remus sighted six vultures over the Aventine Hill, then Romulus saw a flight of twelve above the Palatine Hill') and a translation of Livy 1.7. Clue 3: Wikipedia: twins added in the late 15th century, 'probably by sculptor Antonio del Pollaiuolo' (c. 1471); radiocarbon testing in 2007 gave 1021-1153 AD at 95% confidence. The medieval date is still contested, so the clue says 'suggest'. Clue 4: Remus was killed 'either by Romulus or by one of his supporters' in some versions; the common Livy version has Romulus kill him, so 'one later killed the other' follows the standard story. Both twin names and the full answer are absent from all clues.

clues.text: A descendant of John Fitch, whose steamboat was the first patented in the U.S., patented this appliance in 1886; her version cleaned with water pressure instead of scrubbers.
Chicago's Palmer House hotel made the first big purchase of this invention in 1887, and at the 1893 World's Fair it won a prize for mechanical construction and durability.
This appliance's Illinois inventor was reportedly fed up with servants chipping her heirloom china, and vowed that if nobody else would invent it, she'd do it herself.
About three-quarters of U.S. homes have this kitchen appliance, which sprays hot, soapy water over racks of plates, glasses and cutlery.

dishwasher.writerNotes: Clue 1: sources disagree on how Josephine Cochrane was related to John Fitch. USPTO says maternal grandfather, IEEE Spectrum says great-grandfather, and a 1913 obituary says her mother was a direct descendant. Hence 'a descendant'. Her patent, No. 355,139, was issued in December 1886. Wikipedia, IEEE and USPTO all say her design used water pressure instead of scrubbers. I dropped 'the first to', because Wikipedia's dishwasher article says Houghton's 1850 machine already sprayed water. Clue 2: the Palmer House as first big sale in 1887 comes from USPTO. The prize wording 'best mechanical construction, durability and adaptation to its line of work' is from Wikipedia and USPTO. Clue 3: USPTO and IEEE give the quote 'If nobody else is going to invent a dishwashing machine, I'll do it myself', and both describe servants chipping heirloom china. Clue 4: about 75% of U.S. households, from Wikipedia citing EIA 2015. The alias 'Dishwashing machine' bans 'machine', so the clues say 'appliance', 'invention' and 'plates' instead of 'machine' and 'dishes'.

clues.text: This company began as Fredrik Idestam's 1865 pulp mill in Tampere and took its name from the nearby town where he opened a second mill in 1868.
Long before phones, this company's name was a brand of rubber boots made by the Finnish Rubber Works, which merged with it in 1967; its tyre arm split off in 1988.
A 2009 estimate said this company's signature ringtone, taken from Francisco Tárrega's 1902 guitar piece 'Gran Vals', was heard about 20,000 times a second.
This Finnish brand's famously indestructible 3310, released in 2000, sold about 126 million units and came loaded with the game Snake II.

nokia.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia Nokia: founded 12 May 1865; 'mining engineer Fredrik Idestam established a pulp mill' on the Tammerkoski rapids in Tampere; 'A second pulp mill was opened in 1868 near the neighboring town of Nokia'; company named Nokia Ab 'after the site of the second pulp mill'. Clue 2: Wikipedia Nokia: 'In 1967, the three companies - Nokia, Kaapelitehdas, and Finnish Rubber Works - merged to create a new Nokia Corporation.' Nokian Footwear: Finnish Rubber Works moved to Nokia and 'soon after... began to use the brand Nokia' on its galoshes/boots. Nokian Tyres: began as a Finnish Rubber Works division (tyres from 1932); 'Nokia Corporation's tyre division was separated in 1988 as Nokia Tyres Limited'. Tyres were dropped from the boots half of the clue because I found no source that Finnish Rubber Works' tyres carried the Nokia brand. Clue 3: Wikipedia Nokia tune: excerpt of Gran Vals (1902), bars 13-16; 'A 2009 report estimated it was heard 1.8 billion times per day, about 20,000 times per second.' Clue 4: Wikipedia 3310: released Q4 2000, 126 million sold, shipped with Snake II.

clues.text: This gadget took shape after Apple's Jon Rubinstein was shown a tiny 1.8-inch hard drive at Toshiba in 2001 and promised to buy every one the company could make.
This device's scroll wheel was inspired by a Bang & Olufsen cordless phone, the BeoCom 6000, which Phil Schiller reportedly brought to an early meeting with Steve Jobs.
Copywriter Vinnie Chieco proposed this device's name after its white prototype reminded him of '2001: A Space Odyssey' and the line 'Open the pod bay doors, Hal'.
Steve Jobs unveiled this Apple music player in October 2001 as '1,000 songs in your pocket', and the line ended in May 2022 with the discontinued Touch model.

ipod.writerNotes: Clue 1: IEEE Spectrum: Toshiba hosts 'trotted out a 1.8-inch hard drive' they weren't sure what to do with, and 'Rubinstein told his Toshiba colleagues he'd buy every 1.8-inch drive the company could make.' Computer History Museum: Toshiba MK5002MAL 1.8-inch drive was the first iPod's storage; Rubinstein: 'The key element was the drive.' Date: Isaacson (via Time) puts the visit in February 2001, other accounts January 2001; both are 2001. Clue 2: Tony Fadell tweeted on 10 May 2022 that the wheel was inspired by a B&O DECT cordless phone brought to the first meeting with Jobs; ifun.de names the BeoCom 6000 and says Schiller brought it; ifanr summarises Fast Company's insider quote ('Phil had seen it, and said, Well, we should do that'). Hedged with 'reportedly'. The 2001 original had a mechanically rotating wheel (the 'click wheel' came later), so the clue says 'scroll wheel'. Clue 3: 'pod' is not a leak (the 4-letter answer 'ipod' only matches as a whole word). Clue 4: Wikipedia: discontinued 10 May 2022, iPod Touch being the last model; Apple's newsroom post says 'available while supplies last'.

clues.text: Simon Coencas, one of four boys who found this prehistoric site in 1940, was later interned at Drancy with his Jewish family; he was the last of the four when he died in 2020.
Culture minister André Malraux closed this site to the public in 1963 after visitors' breath and electric lighting set green algae growing on its walls.
A beast at the head of a procession in this site's Hall of the Bulls, drawn with a catlike body and two straight horns, is nicknamed 'the Unicorn'.
Found in 1940 after a teenager's dog nosed into a hole left by a fallen tree, this cave in France's Dordogne is covered with Ice Age images of horses, bulls and stags.

lascaux.writerNotes: Clue 1: the French Ministry of Culture's Lascaux site says Coencas was arrested with his family in 1942 and held at the Muette camp in Drancy. The Red Cross got him and his sister released; other relatives were murdered at Auschwitz. He died on 2 February 2020 as the last of the four discoverers. The ministry's 'four discoverers' page wrongly says the family was deported to Buchenwald, so I avoided naming a camp other than Drancy. His age in 1940 is given as 13 on one ministry page and 15 on another, so I wrote 'boys'. Clue 2: Futura-Sciences says Malraux closed it in April 1963, and that electric lighting plus visitors' breath (moisture, CO2, heat) caused green algae. Wikipedia confirms the 1963 closure and the visitor damage. Clue 3: the ministry describes the 'Unicorn' leading the animals on the wall, with wavy, catlike lines and two straight horns. Clue 4: Wikipedia says Marcel Ravidat (18 by Wikipedia, 17 by the ministry, hence 'a teenager') found the entrance after his dog investigated a hole left by an uprooted tree. Ravidat later embellished this into the dog falling in, so the clue avoids that version. Wikipedia dates the art to about 17,000 to 22,000 years ago. The aliases ban 'cave' and 'paintings'; 'cave' appears only as the kind-word 'this cave' in clue 4.

clues.text: In 2015 the Chinese oil city of Karamay built a mirrored 'oil bubble' so like this artwork that its creator cried plagiarism; the mayor of its home city called the copy flattery.
This artwork's creator sued the NRA in 2018 for showing it in a promotional video, and that December the gun group settled by agreeing to remove the image.
This sculpture's 168 stainless steel plates were welded together and polished until no seams showed; its 110-short-ton form was inspired by liquid mercury.
Anish Kapoor's mirrored sculpture in Chicago's Millennium Park is better known by a nickname that he once called 'completely stupid'.

cloud-gate.writerNotes: Alias 'The Bean' normalizes to 'bean', so that word is banned; clue 4 refers to 'a nickname' instead. Clue 1: Hyperallergic (12 Aug 2015): Karamay sculpture promoted as 'a giant, stainless steel drop of oil'; Kapoor 'shocked at the blatant plagiarism'. Hurriyet: 'in the shape of an oil bubble'. Rahm Emanuel to the Sun-Times: ''Imitation is the greatest form of flattery' is what I would say' (Hyperallergic follow-up). Clue 2: Wikipedia: June 2017 NRA video used an image of the sculpture; Kapoor sued (June 2018); settled December 2018 with the image removed. Apollo (6 Dec 2018) confirms the out-of-court settlement. Sources disagree on the video's name and release month, so the clue names neither. NRA said it paid Kapoor nothing. Clue 3: Wikipedia: 168 plates 3/8 in thick, no visible seams, 110 short tons (100 t), design 'inspired by liquid mercury'. Clue 4: Wikipedia: during construction Kapoor called the nickname 'completely stupid', later accepted it.

clues.text: The first name of this snack's mustachioed mascot, Julius, began as a 2006 Wikipedia prank by a college student who was watching NFL star Julius Peppers.
In 2009 Britain's Court of Appeal ruled that this snack, only about 42% potato, counted as a potato crisp and so owed VAT, overturning its maker's earlier win.
Procter & Gamble chemist Fred Baur, who designed this snack's container, had part of his ashes buried in one after his death in 2008.
Now owned by Mars, this stackable snack's saddle-shaped chips, each a hyperbolic paraboloid, come nested in a tall cardboard tube.

pringles.writerNotes: Clue 1: Input/Inverse says that in 2006 college freshman Justin Shillock added 'Julius Pringles' to Wikipedia after his roommate, who was watching Julius Peppers, joked it as the mascot's name. Wikipedia says Kellogg's acknowledged the name in 2013 (it trademarked 'Julius Pringles' and 'Mr. P'). Clue 2: Court of Appeal ruling of 20 May 2009 (Lord Justice Jacob), reversing the 2008 High Court ruling for P&G. The 42% potato figure is from Improbable Research and Wikipedia. Clue 3: AP (via ABC7) and Wikipedia say Baur died 4 May 2008 and his children buried part of his ashes in a Pringles can, at his request. Clue 4: Mars completed its purchase of Kellanova, which owns Pringles, on 11 December 2025 (Simpson Thacher). The hyperbolic paraboloid shape is from Wikipedia. I avoided 'Pringle Drive' and every other 'Pringle' word.

clues.text: In 2016 a Vanderbilt engineer used a roughly $40 machine for making this treat, bought at Target, to spin fibers that served as molds for artificial capillaries.
The French call this treat 'daddy's beard', and a Paris-based couple borrowed that name in 1970 for Barbapapa, their shape-shifting cartoon hero.
A Nashville dentist co-invented the machine for this treat, and at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair he and his partner sold 68,655 boxes at 25 cents, nearly half the price of admission.
This fluffy fairground treat is made by melting sugar and flinging it through tiny holes, where it cools into hair-thin threads that are wound onto a paper cone.

cotton-candy.writerNotes: Aliases ban 'candy', 'floss' and 'fairy' as well as 'cotton', so the 1904 trade name ('Fairy Floss') is left out. Clue 1: VUMC Reporter (8 Feb 2016): Leon Bellan, Vanderbilt mechanical engineering, bought the machine 'at a Target store for roughly $40'; it spun polymer fibers that were set in gelatin and dissolved to leave channels, a 3D artificial capillary system keeping cells 'viable and functional for more than a week' (Advanced Healthcare Materials, Feb 2016). Clue 2: Wikipedia Barbapapa: from French barbe à papa, 'literally Daddy's beard', meaning cotton candy; creators Annette Tison and Talus Taylor, a French-American couple living in Paris; book published 1970. Smithsonian also lists 'Papa's beard' (France). Clue 3: Wikipedia: 68,655 boxes at 25¢ at the 1904 World's Fair; Gizmodo: dentist William Morrison and confectioner John C. Wharton, 68,655 boxes over 184 days at 25 cents, 'nearly half the fair's admission price'; Smithsonian says 'half'; Morrison was a Nashville dentist (Smithsonian, Gizmodo). Guinness rounds to about 68,000 and one outlet says 65,655 (likely a typo). Clue 4: Smithsonian describes the machine: melted sugar is sprayed through tiny holes by centrifugal force and cools into strands.

clues.text: This computer game was wiped from its school's system at the end of a 1971 term, leaving only a paper printout, and its creator retyped the code over Thanksgiving weekend in 1974.
This game was first played in a Minneapolis history class on a screenless teletype, and players hunted for food by typing 'BANG' as fast as they could.
For a 1975 release, this game's designer set the odds of misfortunes such as illness and death using the diaries and accounts of real 19th-century settlers.
In this classroom computer game, players lead a wagon party west from Independence, Missouri, ford rivers, and often read 'You have died of dysentery.'

oregon-trail.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia says the district deleted the program at semester's end after the team printed its roughly 800 lines of code, and that Rawitsch put it on MECC's system over Thanksgiving weekend in 1974. The MECC history page says Rawitsch himself deleted it and took the printout home. Since the sources differ on who deleted it, the clue says it was 'wiped from its school's system'. Clue 2: it was first played on 3 December 1971 at Bryant Junior High in Minneapolis (MECC); Wikipedia names Jordan Junior High in one place, so the clue says only 'a Minneapolis history class'. The teletype had no screen, and the hunting prompt was 'Type BANG' (MECC, Wikipedia). Clue 3: for the 1975 MECC release, Wikipedia says event probabilities were based on historical diaries and narratives, and MECC says illness, death and water shortages were drawn from settlers' journals. I skipped the lead that Prince was a student at the school, because sources say it is unknown whether he ever played. The words 'Oregon' and 'trail' appear in no clue.

clues.text: In February 2014 Apple and Google began rejecting new games that used this game's distinctive first word, to stem a flood of copycats.
After this game was pulled, phones that still had it installed were listed on eBay with bids reaching $90,000, though many bids were thought to be fake.
Vietnamese developer Dong Nguyen said this game was earning about $50,000 a day from ads when he pulled it in February 2014, tweeting 'I cannot take this anymore.'
In this 2013 mobile game, each tap of the screen keeps a little flier named Faby aloft as it squeezes through gaps between green, Mario-style pipes.

flappy-bird.writerNotes: Clue 1: The Next Web (15/16 Feb 2014): 'Google and Apple are now actively rejecting other games that contain 'Flappy' in the title', 'an apparent effort to stem the flow of clones'. Apple told The Verge the crackdown covered any app trying to trade on a popular original, not just the word. Clue 2: Wikipedia: phones with it pre-installed sold on eBay for $1,499 or more, 'some bids over $90,000'; Digit: an iPhone 5 listing at $90,000 'had 62 bids (which can obviously be fake bids)'. Listings were later removed. Hence the hedge. Clue 3: Wikipedia + bit-tech: ~$50,000 a day from in-app ads (Nguyen's own figure per Wikipedia); tweet 8 Feb 2014 'I cannot take this anymore'; removed 9/10 Feb 2014 (sources differ by a day, so the clue says only February). Clue 4: released iOS 24 May 2013; Wikipedia gameplay: Faby 'only ascends when the player taps the touchscreen', pairs of pipes with gaps; Kotaku criticized 'Mario-style graphics' and called the green pipe 'a new albeit unoriginal drawing'.

clues.text: One of the world's oldest known fishing nets, found in a bog at Antrea, then part of Finland, was made from this tree's fibres more than 10,000 years ago.
Napoleon was first buried on St Helena in a valley shaded by these trees, and visitors took so many cuttings as relics that their offspring are said to grow worldwide.
Linnaeus named one species of this tree 'babylonica' after Psalm 137, whose exiles hang their harps on its branches, though those trees were probably poplars.
Cricket bats are made from the wood of this tree, and its Latin name, Salix, gave us salicylic acid, the basis of aspirin.

willow.writerNotes: Clue 1: the date of the Antrea Net varies by source: about 8540 BC (Wikipedia, Antrea Net), 8300 BC (Wikipedia, Fishing net), 8600 to 8400 BC (History.com). All are more than 10,000 years ago. Wikipedia calls it 'one of the oldest known fishing nets', and History.com calls it the oldest. Antrea is now Kamennogorsk in Russia, hence 'then part of Finland'. The year it was found is given as 1913 or 1914, so I left it out. Clue 2: Babylonstoren and Region Canberra say Napoleon was first buried in the Sane Valley beneath willows, and that visitors took many cuttings that were planted around the world. The worldwide-descendants part is partly legend (region.com.au), hence 'are said to'. Clue 3: Wikipedia says Linnaeus named Salix babylonica believing it was the tree of Psalm 137, but the trees there were Euphrates poplars. The KJV reads 'We hanged our harps upon the willows'. Clue 4: Wikipedia's cricket bat article (cricket bat willow, Salix alba var. caerulea) and its salicylic acid article (name from Latin salix; acetylating it gives aspirin). The aliases ban 'tree' and 'weeping'; 'tree' appears only as the kind-word 'this tree' or 'these trees', and 'trees' in clue 3 refers to the Psalm's trees.

clues.text: In 2015 a palaeontologist at a market in Myitkyina, Myanmar, spotted a 99-million-year-old feathered dinosaur tail in a lump of this, which had been taken for a plant.
This material's ancient Greek name, ēlektron, gave us the word 'electricity', because rubbing it makes it attract light things such as bits of paper.
Prussia's king gave Peter the Great a room paneled in this in 1716; called the 'Eighth Wonder of the World', it was looted by the Nazis in 1941 and never found.
In 'Jurassic Park', scientists clone dinosaurs from blood inside a mosquito preserved in this golden fossilized tree resin.

amber.writerNotes: Leak rule: avoided 'chamber', 'Amberley', 'ambergris' and the name 'Amber Room'. Clue 1: Asian Scientist (Dec 2016): Xing Lida found it in 2015 at 'an amber market in Myitkyina, Myanmar'; it was initially taken for 'some kind of plant inclusion'; ~99 million years old. Xing et al., Current Biology 2016 (Bristol research portal): mid-Cretaceous (~99 Ma) amber from Kachin State; feathered tail of a putative juvenile coelurosaur. Asian Scientist says it was initially taken for a plant inclusion, hence 'had been taken for a plant' (search snippets say the seller thought so, but I did not open those pages). Clue 2: Wikipedia Etymology of electricity: Greek ēlektron 'amber' -> Latin electrum -> Gilbert's 'electricus' (1600); an 'Electrick' attracts light bodies such as bits of paper when rubbed. Clue 3: Wikipedia Amber Room: Frederick William I gave it to Peter the Great in 1716; called the 'Eighth Wonder of the World'; dismantled by Army Group North in 1941 and taken to Königsberg; its fate is unknown (a Soviet report says destroyed April 1945), replica installed 2003. Clue 4: Wikipedia Amber: preserved organisms in amber are a key plot point in Crichton's 1990 novel and the 1993 film.

clues.text: Momus's 1991 album 'Hippopotamomus' cast this figure as a rubber-fetish icon; after his owners threatened legal action, unsold copies were destroyed.
This figure debuted on an 1898 poster raising a goblet of nails and broken glass under a Latin toast from Horace meaning 'Now is the time to drink'.
Aimed at wealthy early motorists, this figure first wore pince-nez and smoked a cigar; he later gave up both and was slimmed down in 1998.
This roly-poly mascot of a French tyre company is built from a stack of white tyres, since tyres were pale until carbon was added to the rubber around 1912.

michelin-man.writerNotes: Clue 1: the Hippopotamomus article says Momus was 'threatened with legal action' by Michelin, that unsold copies were destroyed, and that later pressings dropped the song. The Michelin Man article says Michelin 'sued' him, so I used the more cautious 'threatened legal action'. Clue 2: I could not quote the Latin 'Nunc est bibendum', because 'bibendum' is the alias. Michelin's own pages and Wikipedia confirm the 1898 O'Galop poster, the goblet of nails and broken glass, and the Horace source; 'now is the time to drink' is Michelin's own gloss. Clue 3: Wikipedia says he had pince-nez and a cigar, no longer smoked by the 1960s, and was slimmed down and shown without glasses in 1998. Michelin says the early look was aimed at wealthy car buyers. Clue 4: Wikipedia says tyres were grey-white or beige until carbon was added in 1912, and Michelin says he stays white to evoke natural rubber. Other sources date carbon black to 1910-1912, hence 'around 1912'. No clue has a word beginning with 'man' (the 'man' in the answer).

clues.text: When Ed Headrick, who patented the grooves on this toy's professional model, died in 2002, his ashes were molded into a limited run of them, as he had wished.
Selling an early plastic version of this toy at fairs around 1948, its inventor joked that it was free but the 'invisible wire' it flew on cost $1.
In 1974 a college student sneaked his whippet, Ashley, onto the field at a televised Dodgers game, where the dog leapt to catch these until both were escorted off.
Wham-O named this toy after the Frisbie pie company of Bridgeport, Connecticut, whose empty tins New England college students had long tossed around.

frisbee.writerNotes: Clue 1: PDGA: after redesigning the Pluto Platter into the Professional Model he 'filed a new patent application that claimed the grooves' ('The Lines of Headrick'); on his death in 2002 'his ashes were molded into a limited number of discs per his wishes'. Wikipedia Frisbee also says his ashes were molded into memorial discs. Kept 'disc golf' out of clue 1 because it would give the answer away. Clue 2: Wikipedia Frisbee: Morrison and Franscioni's Flyin-Saucer (from 1948), pitch: 'The Flyin' Saucer is free, but the invisible wire is $1.00.' Flying Disc Museum timeline: sold 1948-50 at fairs, stores and beaches 'using invisible wire and other sales ploys'. Clue 3: Wikipedia Ashley Whippet: Alex Stein, 19-year-old college student, 5 Aug 1974, nationally televised Dodgers-Reds game; Wikipedia says about eight minutes, but an LA Times account (quoted by Dodger Thoughts) suggests a shorter stint, so the clue gives no duration. Clue 4: Wikipedia: named after a Connecticut pie maker whose tins Yale students tossed; New England Historical Society: Frisbie Pie Company founded 1871 in Bridgeport; students across New England campuses tossed the tins; Wham-O changed the spelling from 'Frisbie'. Year of the rename differs (June 1957 per Wikipedia, 1958 per NEHS), so the clue gives none.

clues.text: This NASA robot's wheels are punched with holes that spell 'JPL' in Morse code, leaving tracks its software uses to measure how far it has driven.
Clara Ma, a 12-year-old Kansas sixth-grader, named this robot in a 2009 NASA essay contest and won a trip to sign her name on it while it was being built.
On its first anniversary in August 2013, this robot used vibrations from its soil-analysis instrument to hum 'Happy Birthday' to itself, a stunt it never repeated.
This car-sized, nuclear-powered NASA explorer was lowered onto Mars by a rocket-powered 'sky crane' in August 2012 and has been climbing Mount Sharp in Gale Crater.

curiosity.writerNotes: Clue 1: NASA PIA16112 caption: holes leave imprints that are Morse code for JPL and feed the visual odometry software that measures distance between drive steps. Clue 2: JPL news release (May 2009): sixth-grader, 12, Sunflower Elementary, Lenexa, Kansas; over 9,000 entries; prize was a trip to JPL to sign her name on the rover; Wikipedia states she did sign it. Clue 3: Nextgov 2017 quotes the rover's account: 'I only hummed Happy Birthday to myself once, back in 2013'; the SAM instrument was programmed to vibrate to the tune (on 5 Aug 2013). Clue 4: NASA mission page: landed 6 Aug 2012 (UTC), car-size, explores Gale Crater and Mount Sharp; Wikipedia: sky crane landing, MMRTG plutonium power. The clues avoid 'rover' (a word from the alias) and 'curious'.

clues.text: This mission's command module pilot radioed a day after launch that he hadn't filed his income tax return, and he qualified for an extension as a US citizen 'abroad'.
This mission's plutonium generator, meant to power science experiments on the Moon, came home instead and sank into the Pacific's Tonga Trench.
This mission's crew held the record for the farthest humans had ever traveled from Earth, 400,171 km, until Artemis II passed it on April 6, 2026.
After an oxygen tank exploded on this 1970 Moon mission, Jack Swigert radioed 'Houston, we've had a problem', and the crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat.

apollo-13.writerNotes: Clue 1: Space.com (2020): about 24 h 18 min into the mission Swigert asked 'have you guys completed your income tax?'; he was 'considered a U.S. citizen abroad, which qualified him for an extension'. A 60-day figure appears only in one anecdotal column, so the clue gives no length. Clue 2: the SNAP-27 RTG fuel cask rode home on the LM and was targeted into the Tonga Trench; depth is given variously as 6-9 km (RTG article) or 10 km (Apollo 13 article), so no depth in the clue. Sampling found no plutonium release. Clue 3: Al Jazeera (6 Apr 2026): Artemis II passed Apollo 13's 400,171 km (248,655 mi) record at 15:58 GMT; Wikipedia agrees the record stood until Artemis II's 2026 flyby. Clue 4: Wikipedia quotes Swigert's 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here'; the clue's shortened quote matches the familiar phrasing. Decoys avoid other Apollo numbers because of the matcher.

clues.text: This athlete's older brother Mack won silver in the 200 metres at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, finishing 0.4 seconds behind Jesse Owens.
As an Army lieutenant at Camp Hood, Texas, in 1944, this athlete refused a bus driver's order to move to the back; he was court-martialed and acquitted.
This athlete became UCLA's first four-sport letterman, though in baseball, his weakest sport there, he hit just .097 in his one season.
On April 15, 1947, this Brooklyn Dodger broke Major League Baseball's color line, and every player now wears his No. 42 on that date each year.

jackie-robinson.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia's Mack Robinson article says he took 200 m silver 0.4 seconds behind Jesse Owens. Clue 2: American Heritage says the bus incident was on 6 July 1944 at Camp (Fort) Hood, and a panel of nine officers acquitted him on 2 August 1944. The bus charges themselves were dropped and he was tried on insubordination charges from the confrontation that followed, so 'court-martialed and acquitted' is accurate but compresses the story. The bus was a civilian bus running on the post; UCLA calls it a 'military bus', so the clue just says 'a bus'. Clue 3: UCLA Athletics calls him the school's 'first four-sport letterwinner' and gives his .097 average in his one baseball season (1940). Clue 4: debut on 15 April 1947 with the Brooklyn Dodgers; No. 42 was retired across MLB in 1997, and every player has worn it on April 15 since 2004 (Wikipedia). The words 'Jackie' and 'Robinson' appear in no clue; Mack is named by first name only.

clues.text: This sport's best-known nickname was trademarked in 1901 by the London games maker J. Jaques & Son, which sold the American rights to Parker Brothers.
In 2000 this sport's governing body swapped its 38 mm ball for a 40 mm one, whose extra air resistance slowed rallies down for TV viewers.
In Nagoya in 1971, American player Glenn Cowan rode the Chinese team's bus and got a silk portrait from their star Zhuang Zedong; China soon invited the US team over.
Born as a Victorian after-dinner parlor game with a row of books for a net, this paddle sport has been in the Olympics since Seoul 1988.

table-tennis.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia and NBC: J. Jaques & Son Ltd trademarked 'ping-pong' in 1901 and sold the US rights to Parker Brothers, which enforced it in the 1920s. Clue 2: Wikipedia: 38 mm balls replaced by 40 mm in October 2000, increasing air resistance and slowing the game, which had become too fast to watch on television; the KTH document cites ITTF aims of longer rallies and better TV visibility. Clue 3: Wikipedia (Ping-pong diplomacy) and NPR (2013 obituary of Zhuang): Cowan missed his team's bus and rode the Chinese one; Zhuang gave him a silk-screen portrait of the Huangshan mountains; Mao then ordered the US team invited. Sources differ on 4 vs 6 April for the bus ride, so no exact date. Clue 4: Wikipedia: Victorian upper-class after-dinner parlour game, books as net; NBC: Olympic debut at Seoul 1988. No clue uses table, tennis, ping or pong.
